questions.q: Why can't a service in an Azure VNet reach a service in an AWS VPC by default?
options: Both clouds block all private traffic between any two VNets or VPCs, even within the same cloud
ExpressRoute and Direct Connect are automatically cross-connected to each other the moment both exist
Azure and AWS are both private networks with no built-in awareness of each other; the path has to be built explicitly
AWS VPCs cannot accept any inbound traffic from outside AWS under any configuration
questions.explain: A VNet and a VPC are each private networks with no default knowledge of the other cloud. Reaching across requires explicitly building either a VPN tunnel or a dedicated circuit path.

questions.q: In a gateway-to-gateway VPN between Azure and AWS, what does enabling BGP on both gateways accomplish?
options: It encrypts the tunnel traffic, which static routing cannot do
It lets each side learn the other's address space automatically, instead of relying on hand-entered static routes
It is required before either cloud will allow a VPN connection to be created at all
It replaces the need for a shared pre-shared key on the tunnel
questions.explain: BGP exchanges routes dynamically between the two gateways, so if either side's subnets change later, routing stays correct without manual static-route updates.

questions.q: What does a colocation meet-point connecting an ExpressRoute circuit and a Direct Connect connection actually achieve?
options: It doubles the available bandwidth of a VPN tunnel without any additional cost
It lets cross-cloud traffic travel entirely over private infrastructure, never touching the public internet
It automatically converts an AWS VPC into an Azure VNet for billing purposes
It removes the need for BGP or any routing configuration between the two clouds
questions.explain: A cross-connect inside a shared connectivity-provider facility joins the two dedicated circuits directly, so traffic never has to cross the public internet at any point.

questions.q: Which workload is the better fit for a VPN tunnel rather than a colocation meet-point, based on this lesson?
options: An occasional, moderate-volume API call between services in different clouds
A continuous, high-throughput data replication job between two clouds
A workload that cannot tolerate any variability in available bandwidth
A workload where the dedicated circuit's provisioning lead time is irrelevant
questions.explain: A VPN is cheap and fast to stand up and is the pragmatic default for most service-to-service traffic; a meet-point earns its cost and lead time only for sustained, throughput-sensitive traffic.

questions.q: Why does this lesson configure a VPN tunnel as a failover path alongside a colocation meet-point circuit, rather than relying on the meet-point alone?
options: Because colocation meet-points are always more expensive than VPNs and should be avoided entirely
Because AWS requires every Direct Connect connection to have a VPN backup by policy
Because a VPN tunnel provides higher throughput than any dedicated circuit
Because having two independent paths, not either path alone, is what actually makes the cross-cloud connection resilient
questions.explain: As with hybrid on-prem connectivity, a dedicated circuit is not inherently more reliable than a VPN — resilience comes from having two independent paths so one can fail over to the other.
